explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but no. Luke says Jesus was met by ten lepers, and then he tells us they stood at a distance (Luke 17:12). So the meeting happens, just from way over there. It's like greeting a neighbor from the far end of the street, where everybody's waving and nobody's close enough to shake a hand.

That's it, baker. The ten meet Jesus, but they stood at a distance (Luke 17:12). Nobody walks up for a handshake. It's a meeting where everybody stays at the back of the room and the front row sits empty.

explanations.answer: They raise their voices and shout
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Luke says they "raised their voices, shouting, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!'" (Luke 17:13). No messenger, no middleman. Just ten voices doing the job themselves, and that's a lot of lung power for one road.

explanations.answer: They send a friend to bring Him
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a friend here, baker. The ten do it themselves. Luke says they raised their voices and shouted, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" (Luke 17:13). No go-between needed when you've got ten voices.

explanations.answer: They wave until He comes over
explanations.explanation: Waving is a good guess, friend, but Luke doesn't mention any waving. He says they raised their voices, shouting, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" (Luke 17:13). Waving from a distance can get lost fast, but a shout carries.

Mercy it is, friend. They shout, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" (Luke 17:13). Notice they don't hand Him a long list. It's one short request, and they shout it loud enough to reach Him from where they stand.
Good thought, but money isn't in the text, baker. Luke records the shout: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" (Luke 17:13). The word they use is mercy. Nobody brings up a price tag.

Shelter makes sense as a guess, friend, but it's not what they ask for. The shout in Luke is, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" (Luke 17:13). Mercy is the word on their lips. That's the whole request.

explanations.answer: Go show yourselves to the priests
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker! Jesus tells them, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." (Luke 17:14). Notice He doesn't say come over here first. He gives them a direction, and that's it. I'd have wanted a map and a cookie for the road.

explanations.answer: Go wash seven times in the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's a real Bible instruction, friend, but it's from a different story. The prophet Elisha told Naaman, commander of Aram's army, to wash seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:10). Here, Jesus tells the ten, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." (Luke 17:14). Two healings, two sets of directions.

explanations.answer: Come close and touch My cloak
explanations.explanation: Cloak touching is in the Gospels, baker, but not here. A woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years said to herself that if she only touched His cloak she'd be healed (Matthew 9:20-21). With the ten, Jesus says, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." (Luke 17:14). He never asks them to come close.

True, friend! Luke says, "…as they were on their way, they were cleansed." (Luke 17:14). They haven't reached the priests yet. The cleansing shows up mid-walk, like pulling a batch out of the oven and finding the timer still has minutes left.

Not quite, baker. Luke says, "…as they were on their way, they were cleansed." (Luke 17:14). So the cleansing happens during the walk, before they get to the priests. Healing met them out on the road.

Yes, friend! When he saw that he was healed, he came back, praising God (Luke 17:15). Everybody had been walking one way, and he turns around. That's a U-turn, and I bet there's a whole lot of joy behind it.

explanations.answer: He hurries on to the priests
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. Luke says this man saw that he was healed and came back, praising God in a loud voice (Luke 17:15). He turns toward Jesus, not away. Going to the priests is where they were headed, but he heads back.

explanations.answer: He goes home to his family
explanations.explanation: Going home is a nice thought, friend, but Luke never says it. He says the man saw he was healed and came back, praising God in a loud voice (Luke 17:15). His first move is to turn around. Home isn't mentioned.
True, baker! He came back, "…praising God in a loud voice." (Luke 17:15). That's no whisper and no polite little nod. This man has no indoor voice, and I love it.
Not this time, friend. Luke says he came back, "…praising God in a loud voice." (Luke 17:15). So he's loud about it. No whisper in that praise.

That's what the ten did at the start, friend, but this man does something different. He fell facedown at Jesus' feet in thanksgiving (Luke 17:16). Facedown at His feet is about as close as you can get. The ten stood at a distance and raised their voices (Luke 17:12-13), and he ends up right there.

Right, baker! The ten stood at a distance in the beginning (Luke 17:12). Now this man falls facedown at Jesus' feet in thanksgiving (Luke 17:16). He goes from a long-distance shout to as close as it gets.
Yes, friend! Luke says, "…and he was a Samaritan." (Luke 17:16). Later Jesus calls him "this foreigner" (Luke 17:18). So the one who came back is the Samaritan.

Galilee does show up in this story, baker, since Jesus is passing between Samaria and Galilee (Luke 17:11). But Luke says of this man, "…and he was a Samaritan." (Luke 17:16). Jesus even calls him "this foreigner" (Luke 17:18). Good guess, just a different region.

Judean is a fair guess, friend, but Luke doesn't use it here. He says, "…and he was a Samaritan." (Luke 17:16). Jesus then calls him "this foreigner" (Luke 17:18). That's the detail Luke gives us about him.
That's it, baker! Jesus asks, "Were not all ten cleansed?" and then, "Where then are the other nine?" (Luke 17:17). The count is right there in His words. Ten were cleansed, and one is at His feet.

explanations.answer: Why did the others not wait
explanations.explanation: That's not what Jesus asks, friend. He asks, "Were not all ten cleansed?" and then, "Where then are the other nine?" (Luke 17:17). He asks where they are. He doesn't ask why, and the text doesn't tell us why either.

explanations.answer: Who told the others to leave
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask that, baker. His questions are, "Were not all ten cleansed?" and "Where then are the other nine?" (Luke 17:17). He's asking where they are. Nobody gets blamed for leaving in that question.

Glory, friend! Jesus asks, "Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?" (Luke 17:18). The man had been praising God in a loud voice (Luke 17:15). That's giving glory, and Jesus puts a name on it.

Tithes is a good guess, baker, but it isn't the word. Jesus says, "Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?" (Luke 17:18). The word is glory. Nothing in the passage mentions tithes.

Sacrifices isn't the word Jesus uses, friend. He says, "Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?" (Luke 17:18). Glory is what Jesus names. Sacrifices never come up in this story.

Faith, baker! Jesus tells him, "Rise and go; your faith has made you well!" (Luke 17:19). That's the last thing Jesus says to this man in the passage. He came back and fell facedown at Jesus' feet (Luke 17:15-16), and those are the words Jesus gives him.
Close, friend, since the man really did praise God in a loud voice (Luke 17:15). But Jesus' words are, "Rise and go; your faith has made you well!" (Luke 17:19). The word He picks is faith.

Courage sounds right for a man who falls facedown at Jesus' feet, baker, but it's not what Jesus says. His words are, "Rise and go; your faith has made you well!" (Luke 17:19). Faith is the word. Courage never appears in this passage.
